patterns.name: Discriminated Union
patterns.problem: a domain value can be in one of several mutually exclusive states and illegal combinations must be unrepresentable
patterns.exampleContext: a checkout workflow whose pending, authorized, captured, failed, and refunded states currently share a bag of optional fields
patterns.mechanism: a closed union with a stable discriminant, state-specific payloads, exhaustive narrowing, and explicit transition functions
patterns.simplerAlternative: a class hierarchy when behavior and extension by third parties dominate over closed data variants
patterns.misuse: creating a giant union that centralizes unrelated domains or using an open string discriminant that destroys exhaustiveness
patterns.evidence: compile-time rejection of illegal states, exhaustive transition coverage, branch complexity, and ease of adding a new state
patterns.typescript: literal types, `never` exhaustiveness checks, `satisfies`, narrowing, readonly payloads, and strict compiler options

patterns.name: Result
patterns.problem: expected failure must be represented explicitly without exceptions erasing the contract
patterns.exampleContext: a payment-adapter pipeline with validation, provider rejection, timeout, and infrastructure failure
patterns.mechanism: a discriminated success/failure value with typed error variants and combinators that preserve causality
patterns.simplerAlternative: exceptions for truly exceptional faults or a rejected Promise at an infrastructure boundary
patterns.misuse: wrapping every operation in Result until ordinary code becomes ceremonial, or collapsing all failures into one string
patterns.evidence: handled failure variants, preserved error causes, unhandled rejection count, control-flow complexity, and caller ergonomics
patterns.typescript: generics, conditional types only when justified, discriminated unions, `unknown` in catch blocks, and async composition

patterns.name: Option
patterns.problem: absence is expected and must not be confused with null, failure, falsy values, or an uninitialized field
patterns.exampleContext: a customer-preference service that currently mixes `undefined`, `null`, empty strings, and lookup failures
patterns.mechanism: an explicit Some/None representation with narrow boundary conversions and composable mapping
patterns.simplerAlternative: plain `T | undefined` when the code path is local, obvious, and does not require composition
patterns.misuse: introducing a monadic wrapper for every optional property or hiding database and network errors as None
patterns.evidence: null-related defects, number of unchecked assertions, branch clarity, and adapter conversion count
patterns.typescript: strict null checks, union narrowing, generics, optional chaining at boundaries, and exhaustive matching

patterns.name: Branded Type
patterns.problem: structurally identical primitives represent different domain concepts and can be accidentally interchanged
patterns.exampleContext: a fulfillment service that mixes customer IDs, order IDs, cents, percentages, timestamps, and unvalidated strings
patterns.mechanism: opaque or branded types created only through validating constructors and removed at serialization boundaries
patterns.simplerAlternative: small Value Objects when runtime behavior, invariants, formatting, or richer semantics justify an object
patterns.misuse: casting with `as` throughout the codebase, branding unvalidated data, or branding every local string
patterns.evidence: invalid cross-assignment caught by the compiler, validation centralization, casts outside constructors, and boundary friction
patterns.typescript: unique symbols, intersections, nominal-brand helpers, assertion functions, and schema-decoder integration

patterns.name: Higher-Order Function
patterns.problem: behavior varies while the surrounding control flow remains stable and a class hierarchy would add needless structure
patterns.exampleContext: an HTTP client that needs pluggable retry, logging, authorization, caching, and transformation behavior
patterns.mechanism: functions accepted, returned, or composed as behavior values with narrow typed contracts
patterns.simplerAlternative: Strategy objects when behavior owns state, lifecycle, multiple related operations, or a discoverable domain identity
patterns.misuse: anonymous wrapper pyramids with invisible ordering, captured mutable state, or types too generic to explain the contract
patterns.evidence: allocation and call overhead where relevant, stack trace quality, compositional clarity, test isolation, and change locality
patterns.typescript: generic call signatures, overload restraint, closures, variadic tuples, async functions, and preserved error types

patterns.name: Composition Root
patterns.problem: object construction, configuration, and infrastructure selection leak into domain behavior
patterns.exampleContext: a multi-tenant API whose handlers instantiate repositories, clocks, queues, and payment clients directly
patterns.mechanism: one explicit application boundary that assembles the dependency graph and selects concrete adapters
patterns.simplerAlternative: a small manual factory in tiny programs where a named root would add no clarity
patterns.misuse: turning the root into a service locator, allowing runtime access from arbitrary modules, or hiding circular dependencies
patterns.evidence: domain imports of infrastructure, graph cycles, test setup size, startup validation, and replacement of adapters
patterns.typescript: typed configuration parsing, explicit constructor functions, module boundaries, `satisfies`, and no global container

patterns.name: Dependency Injection
patterns.problem: business behavior depends on capabilities whose implementations vary across environments or tests
patterns.exampleContext: an invoicing service coupled directly to system time, UUID generation, PostgreSQL, email, and a tax provider
patterns.mechanism: dependencies supplied explicitly through constructors or functions, expressed as minimal capability-oriented ports
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct construction for stable value objects and pure helpers that have no environmental variation
patterns.misuse: injecting every function, adopting a magical reflection container, or exposing a generic dependency bag
patterns.evidence: dependency fan-out, mock count, constructor width, replacement effort, and whether domain tests require infrastructure
patterns.typescript: structural interfaces, type-only imports, readonly dependencies, factory functions, and explicit async lifecycles

patterns.name: Functional Core Imperative Shell
patterns.problem: business decisions are tangled with I/O, time, randomness, retries, and framework callbacks
patterns.exampleContext: a fraud-decision endpoint that reads data, calculates risk, writes decisions, emits events, and calls an external provider
patterns.mechanism: a deterministic core that receives values and returns decisions or effects, surrounded by a thin orchestration shell
patterns.simplerAlternative: a cohesive stateful domain model when identity, invariants, and long-lived behavior are clearer as objects
patterns.misuse: moving all logic into enormous pure functions, modeling every I/O as an abstract effect system, or duplicating orchestration
patterns.evidence: pure-core coverage, shell branch count, deterministic replay, mutation score, and infrastructure-free test runtime
patterns.typescript: readonly data, discriminated effects, pure functions, explicit clocks and random sources, and exhaustiveness

patterns.name: Factory Method
patterns.problem: a stable workflow must choose or defer construction of a varying product
patterns.exampleContext: a document-import pipeline supporting CSV, JSON, XML, and partner-specific formats
patterns.mechanism: a creation hook or typed factory function that returns a common product contract while preserving workflow invariants
patterns.simplerAlternative: a direct constructor or simple map of constructors when creation has no policy or lifecycle
patterns.misuse: one factory per trivial class, factories that merely rename `new`, or returning an unbounded union of unrelated products
patterns.evidence: change locality when adding a format, constructor duplication, invalid construction paths, and test seam quality
patterns.typescript: constructor signatures, generic factory maps, abstract classes only when shared lifecycle exists, and exhaustive keys

patterns.name: Abstract Factory
patterns.problem: families of collaborating objects must vary together without allowing incompatible combinations
patterns.exampleContext: a deployment planner producing provider-specific compute, queue, storage, and observability adapters
patterns.mechanism: a family-level factory contract that creates mutually compatible products behind explicit capability ports
patterns.simplerAlternative: a configuration object plus independent factories when compatibility is enforced elsewhere
patterns.misuse: creating parallel inheritance hierarchies for one product, hiding configuration errors, or supporting hypothetical families
patterns.evidence: invalid family combinations, graph size, onboarding effort for a new provider, and duplicated setup logic
patterns.typescript: mapped types for product families, `satisfies` for complete factories, generics, and explicit lifecycle disposal

patterns.name: Builder
patterns.problem: construction requires ordered stages, many optional choices, validation, or multiple representations
patterns.exampleContext: an observability query builder producing validated trace, log, and metric queries from a shared request model
patterns.mechanism: a separate incremental construction process with a final validation boundary and immutable finished product
patterns.simplerAlternative: a named options object with defaults when order and cross-field invariants are simple
patterns.misuse: fluent APIs that accept impossible sequences, mutable builders reused across requests, or builders for two-field objects
patterns.evidence: invalid intermediate states exposed, configuration defect rate, call-site readability, allocations, and reuse hazards
patterns.typescript: polymorphic `this`, staged generic builders only when they improve safety, readonly output, and runtime schema validation

patterns.name: Prototype
patterns.problem: creating an object from scratch is expensive or variants should inherit a configured baseline at runtime
patterns.exampleContext: a simulation platform cloning scenario graphs containing workloads, failure schedules, and resource budgets
patterns.mechanism: explicit prototype objects with domain-aware clone semantics and controlled deep or structural sharing
patterns.simplerAlternative: a factory or persistent immutable data structure when identity-preserving cloning is unnecessary
patterns.misuse: blind JSON serialization, accidental shared mutable references, copying secrets, or treating cloning as persistence
patterns.evidence: clone correctness, shared-reference defects, memory use, construction latency, and semantic identity rules
patterns.typescript: structured cloning limits, readonly graphs, custom clone contracts, private fields, maps, sets, and branded identities

patterns.name: Singleton
patterns.problem: exactly one coordinated instance is required within a clearly defined runtime scope
patterns.exampleContext: a process-level schema registry used by a compiler worker while tests require isolated registries
patterns.mechanism: scope ownership enforced by the composition root rather than uncontrolled global access
patterns.simplerAlternative: an ordinary object passed explicitly, a module value, or a keyed registry for multi-tenant scopes
patterns.misuse: global mutable state, hidden dependencies, cross-test leakage, false assumptions across workers, or using Singleton for convenience
patterns.evidence: test isolation, initialization races, multi-process behavior, tenant leakage, and dependency visibility
patterns.typescript: ES module caching semantics, workers and processes, explicit lifecycle, `globalThis` hazards, and symbol-keyed registries

patterns.name: Adapter
patterns.problem: an existing or external interface does not match the contract required by the application
patterns.exampleContext: a shipping platform integrating three carriers with incompatible address, label, tracking, and error models
patterns.mechanism: a boundary object that translates operations, data, errors, units, and lifecycle into a stable internal port
patterns.simplerAlternative: a plain conversion function when only one stateless data shape differs
patterns.misuse: leaking provider types inward, swallowing semantic differences, or forcing every provider into a dishonest lowest-common denominator
patterns.evidence: provider-specific imports beyond the boundary, translation defects, change impact, contract-test coverage, and error fidelity
patterns.typescript: structural interfaces, schema parsing of unknown data, error unions, type-only imports, and exhaustive provider mapping

patterns.name: Bridge
patterns.problem: two independent dimensions of variation would otherwise create a combinatorial class hierarchy
patterns.exampleContext: a notification system varying message semantics independently from email, SMS, push, and webhook delivery
patterns.mechanism: separate abstraction and implementation hierarchies joined through a narrow runtime bridge
patterns.simplerAlternative: Strategy when only one behavior axis varies or Adapter when reconciling an existing incompatible interface
patterns.misuse: prematurely separating dimensions that always change together or designing ports so generic that semantics disappear
patterns.evidence: number of combinations without new classes, coupling between dimensions, substitution tests, and configuration clarity
patterns.typescript: generic ports, discriminated configuration, dependency injection, variance awareness, and no nominal hierarchy requirement

patterns.name: Composite
patterns.problem: clients must treat individual objects and recursive groups uniformly
patterns.exampleContext: an authorization-policy engine combining atomic predicates into nested all, any, not, and threshold rules
patterns.mechanism: a tree of components sharing a meaningful operation while containers delegate recursively to children
patterns.simplerAlternative: a discriminated union plus recursive pure function when the set of node types is closed and data-centric
patterns.misuse: forcing leaves to expose meaningless child methods, unbounded recursion, cycles, or hiding expensive tree traversal
patterns.evidence: tree depth, traversal cost, stack safety, invalid cycles, operation uniformity, and ease of adding nodes versus operations
patterns.typescript: recursive types, discriminated unions, readonly children, iterators, cycle guards, and exhaustive evaluation

patterns.name: Decorator
patterns.problem: responsibilities must be combined dynamically without multiplying subclasses or modifying the wrapped component
patterns.exampleContext: an outbound HTTP client needing optional tracing, authentication, caching, retry, metering, and redaction
patterns.mechanism: contract-preserving wrappers that delegate while adding one explicit responsibility and defined ordering semantics
patterns.simplerAlternative: middleware when the operation naturally flows through a shared pipeline or higher-order functions for stateless wrappers
patterns.misuse: order-dependent wrapper stacks nobody can inspect, behavioral contract violations, duplicated caching, or swallowed errors
patterns.evidence: call overhead, stack trace clarity, ordering tests, contract preservation, configuration observability, and wrapper count
patterns.typescript: generic delegation, function decorators, class decorators only with clear semantics, symbols, and preserved `this` binding

patterns.name: Facade
patterns.problem: clients need a stable, intention-revealing entry point over a complicated subsystem
patterns.exampleContext: a media-processing subsystem coordinating upload, transcoding, metadata, storage, moderation, and publishing
patterns.mechanism: a coarse use-case-oriented interface that coordinates subsystem capabilities without hiding necessary operational outcomes
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct subsystem access for expert internal clients that genuinely need its full flexibility
patterns.misuse: a god service containing business logic, suppressing failure detail, or freezing all clients to one oversized interface
patterns.evidence: client dependency count, orchestration duplication, facade width, change propagation, and failure transparency
patterns.typescript: narrow exported types, module export control, Result unions, async cancellation, and explicit dependency construction

patterns.name: Flyweight
patterns.problem: a very large number of logically distinct objects repeat immutable intrinsic state
patterns.exampleContext: a syntax-highlighting engine representing millions of tokens that share grammar, style, and category metadata
patterns.mechanism: shared immutable intrinsic objects combined with externally supplied extrinsic context
patterns.simplerAlternative: ordinary allocation until profiling proves memory pressure, or value interning built into the runtime
patterns.misuse: sharing mutable state, interning unbounded user input, memory leaks in caches, or increasing CPU to save irrelevant memory
patterns.evidence: heap retained size, allocation rate, lookup overhead, cache cardinality, and correctness under shared use
patterns.typescript: readonly objects, WeakMap where ownership fits, symbol tables, canonicalization maps, and explicit cache bounds

patterns.name: Proxy
patterns.problem: access to an object requires control such as laziness, remoting, authorization, caching, or monitoring
patterns.exampleContext: a document repository that may be local or remote and requires access checks, caching, and request telemetry
patterns.mechanism: a stand-in preserving the subject contract while controlling access and making remote or delayed semantics explicit
patterns.simplerAlternative: Decorator for added responsibility or Adapter when the underlying contract is incompatible
patterns.misuse: pretending remote calls are local, surprising identity behavior, invisible latency, stale caches, or JavaScript Proxy magic
patterns.evidence: latency visibility, cache correctness, authorization coverage, contract equivalence, and debugging transparency
patterns.typescript: explicit proxy classes versus `Proxy`, async contracts, abort signals, private fields, and reflective-operation traps

patterns.name: Chain of Responsibility
patterns.problem: a request may be handled, transformed, rejected, or passed through an ordered set of independent handlers
patterns.exampleContext: an API request pipeline performing authentication, tenant resolution, validation, quotas, routing, and audit
patterns.mechanism: linked or array-based handlers with explicit continuation, stop semantics, ordering, and observable outcomes
patterns.simplerAlternative: a direct conditional decision table when rules are small, fixed, and must be understood together
patterns.misuse: implicit ordering, multiple handlers acting accidentally, swallowed requests, or shared mutable request context
patterns.evidence: handler coupling, reorder safety, traceability, short-circuit correctness, and per-handler latency
patterns.typescript: typed middleware contexts, discriminated continue/stop results, async composition, variadic tuples, and abort propagation

patterns.name: Command
patterns.problem: a request must become a first-class value that can be queued, logged, retried, authorized, or undone
patterns.exampleContext: a collaborative editor processing user operations through history, audit, permission, and offline queues
patterns.mechanism: an explicit command carrying intent with a handler contract and separated execution policy
patterns.simplerAlternative: a direct function call when invocation does not need independent lifecycle or metadata
patterns.misuse: an anemic command class for every call, mixing transport DTOs with domain intent, or assuming undo is always possible
patterns.evidence: queueability, audit completeness, idempotency, handler fan-out, serialization stability, and undo correctness
patterns.typescript: discriminated command unions, typed handler maps, exhaustive registration, branded IDs, and serializable payloads

patterns.name: Interpreter
patterns.problem: a bounded language or rule grammar must be represented and evaluated repeatedly
patterns.exampleContext: a feature-policy language supporting boolean rules, comparisons, membership, tenant attributes, and rollout percentages
patterns.mechanism: an explicit grammar, syntax tree, parser, and interpreter whose semantics are testable independently
patterns.simplerAlternative: a table-driven evaluator, parser generator, or existing standards-based language when the grammar is not truly small
patterns.misuse: inventing an unsafe general-purpose language, ambiguous grammar, uncontrolled recursion, or string evaluation
patterns.evidence: parse error quality, grammar ambiguity, evaluation complexity, denial-of-service limits, and semantic test coverage
patterns.typescript: discriminated AST unions, recursive descent, exhaustive visitors, branded tokens, and `never` checks

patterns.name: Iterator
patterns.problem: clients need sequential or lazy access without depending on collection representation
patterns.exampleContext: an audit-log service reading paginated database rows, archived objects, and live events as one logical sequence
patterns.mechanism: a traversal object or generator that owns cursor state and exposes a stable iteration protocol
patterns.simplerAlternative: an array or eager collection when the data is small and materialization is harmless
patterns.misuse: single-use iterators reused accidentally, resource leaks, hidden network calls per item, or no cancellation/backpressure
patterns.evidence: memory use, time to first item, round trips, cleanup correctness, cancellation latency, and traversal independence
patterns.typescript: `Iterable`, `AsyncIterable`, generators, `return()` cleanup, abort signals, and typed page cursors

patterns.name: Mediator
patterns.problem: many components communicate through a tangled graph of direct dependencies
patterns.exampleContext: a live operations console where filters, selection, charts, traces, logs, and incident state continually coordinate
patterns.mechanism: a mediator owning interaction rules while components expose focused events and operations
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct collaboration for two stable peers or publish-subscribe when no central interaction policy exists
patterns.misuse: a god mediator containing every business rule, stringly typed events, or invisible global event buses
patterns.evidence: dependency edges, mediator complexity, event traceability, change locality, and component reuse
patterns.typescript: typed event maps, exhaustive dispatch, module boundaries, weak references only when justified, and async event sequencing

patterns.name: Memento
patterns.problem: state must be captured and restored without exposing or violating the originator's invariants
patterns.exampleContext: a workflow designer supporting undo, redo, draft recovery, and migration across schema versions
patterns.mechanism: opaque snapshots created and restored by the state owner with explicit retention and versioning
patterns.simplerAlternative: Command-based inverse operations when reversal is cheap, semantic, and more compact than snapshots
patterns.misuse: serializing arbitrary internals, retaining unlimited history, restoring stale external references, or copying secrets
patterns.evidence: snapshot size, restore correctness, retention cost, migration success, and identity consistency
patterns.typescript: readonly snapshot types, structured clone constraints, versioned discriminated schemas, and private restoration APIs

patterns.name: Observer
patterns.problem: multiple dependents must react when a subject changes without the subject knowing their concrete implementations
patterns.exampleContext: a job-execution service notifying progress views, audit, metrics, billing, and user alerts
patterns.mechanism: typed subscription with explicit lifecycle, delivery semantics, error policy, and ordering guarantees
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct calls for a tiny stable set of mandatory reactions or durable messaging across process boundaries
patterns.misuse: memory leaks, reentrant updates, undefined ordering, exception cascades, or confusing in-process events with reliable messaging
patterns.evidence: subscription leaks, delivery latency, error isolation, ordering tests, and observer fan-out
patterns.typescript: typed event maps, unsubscribe handles, AbortSignal integration, weak references with caution, and async listener contracts

patterns.name: State
patterns.problem: behavior changes with lifecycle state and conditionals have spread across operations
patterns.exampleContext: a deployment job moving through queued, provisioning, running, cancelling, failed, and completed states
patterns.mechanism: state-specific behavior and explicit legal transitions represented by objects or a closed transition table
patterns.simplerAlternative: a discriminated union and pure reducer when states are closed and primarily data-oriented
patterns.misuse: one class per trivial enum, transitions scattered inside states, cyclic coupling, or illegal transitions still representable
patterns.evidence: illegal transition rejection, branch complexity, transition coverage, state additions, and observability
patterns.typescript: discriminated unions versus polymorphic states, exhaustive reducers, branded events, and readonly transition tables

patterns.name: Strategy
patterns.problem: a family of interchangeable algorithms must vary independently from the client using them
patterns.exampleContext: a pricing service choosing discount, tax, allocation, and ranking policies by market and experiment
patterns.mechanism: a minimal algorithm contract with explicit selection and independently testable implementations
patterns.simplerAlternative: a higher-order function for small stateless behavior or a decision table for combinatorial business rules
patterns.misuse: one class per tiny conditional, strategies with incompatible preconditions, or selection logic duplicated across callers
patterns.evidence: branch reduction, substitution tests, policy selection clarity, allocation overhead, and frequency of independent change
patterns.typescript: function and object strategies, generic constraints, readonly inputs, exhaustive registries, and typed configuration

patterns.name: Template Method
patterns.problem: several workflows share an invariant algorithm skeleton but differ at controlled steps
patterns.exampleContext: a data-import framework that consistently validates, normalizes, persists, audits, and reports many feed formats
patterns.mechanism: a base workflow fixes sequencing and exposes narrow hooks with documented preconditions and postconditions
patterns.simplerAlternative: composition with injected steps when runtime flexibility and independent testing matter more than inheritance
patterns.misuse: fragile base classes, too many hooks, hooks depending on hidden state, or subclasses violating the algorithm contract
patterns.evidence: override count, hook coupling, subclass defects, change propagation, and ability to test steps independently
patterns.typescript: abstract protected methods, `final` unavailable in TypeScript, constructor hazards, generics, and composition comparison

patterns.name: Visitor
patterns.problem: many operations must be added across a stable family of element types without modifying every element repeatedly
patterns.exampleContext: a query-plan AST requiring validation, optimization, formatting, cost estimation, and execution tracing
patterns.mechanism: double dispatch or exhaustive visitor maps that separate operations from a stable element structure
patterns.simplerAlternative: discriminated unions with exhaustive functions when TypeScript's closed-world data model is simpler
patterns.misuse: using Visitor on a frequently changing element hierarchy, unsafe casts, default cases that defeat exhaustiveness, or cyclic traversal
patterns.evidence: effort to add an operation versus an element, exhaustiveness, traversal duplication, and compiler-detected omissions
patterns.typescript: discriminated unions, mapped visitor types, `never`, generic return types, and class-based double dispatch comparison

patterns.name: Transaction Script
patterns.problem: a business operation needs straightforward orchestration without a rich domain model
patterns.exampleContext: an internal expense-reimbursement service with a small number of mostly independent use cases
patterns.mechanism: one procedure per use case coordinating validation, persistence, authorization, and side effects across explicit boundaries
patterns.simplerAlternative: a Domain Model when rules, invariants, lifecycle, and interactions are becoming the dominant complexity
patterns.misuse: duplicated rules across scripts, transaction scripts calling one another recursively, or embedding SQL and transport concerns everywhere
patterns.evidence: duplication, script length, invariant leakage, transaction duration, and change impact across use cases
patterns.typescript: typed use-case inputs, Result errors, explicit transactions, dependency injection, and schema-validated boundaries

patterns.name: Domain Model
patterns.problem: complex business rules and state transitions need a behavioral model aligned with domain concepts
patterns.exampleContext: a subscription-billing system handling plans, proration, credits, suspensions, renewals, and contractual constraints
patterns.mechanism: entities, values, policies, and services that own invariants and behavior rather than exposing mutable data bags
patterns.simplerAlternative: Transaction Script for simple CRUD-oriented workflows or a functional core for calculation-heavy stateless rules
patterns.misuse: anemic entities, persistence-driven modeling, giant aggregates, framework annotations in the core, or modeling every noun as a class
patterns.evidence: invariant locality, domain-only test coverage, model coupling, transaction boundaries, and concept-to-code traceability
patterns.typescript: private state, readonly values, branded identities, explicit factories, discriminated events, and no infrastructure imports

patterns.name: Service Layer
patterns.problem: clients need a stable application boundary and consistent orchestration of use cases and transactions
patterns.exampleContext: a lending application serving HTTP, scheduled jobs, CLI administration, and message consumers
patterns.mechanism: a use-case-oriented layer defining available operations, transaction boundaries, authorization coordination, and responses
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct domain invocation in a single-interface application where another layer would only forward calls
patterns.misuse: god services, one service per entity, business rules duplicated outside the domain, or transport-specific return types
patterns.evidence: API stability, orchestration duplication, service width, transaction placement, and domain leakage
patterns.typescript: explicit input/output contracts, type-only ports, Result unions, abort signals, and composition-root assembly

patterns.name: Repository
patterns.problem: domain code needs collection-like access to aggregates without depending on persistence technology
patterns.exampleContext: a marketplace domain loading and saving orders across PostgreSQL while tests use controlled in-memory storage
patterns.mechanism: an aggregate-oriented persistence port with domain-language queries and no generic CRUD leakage
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct typed SQL in simple data-centric services where a repository would merely obscure useful queries
patterns.misuse: generic repositories, returning persistence rows, leaking query builders, N+1 behavior, or pretending remote access is free
patterns.evidence: domain-to-database coupling, query count, aggregate consistency, contract-test parity, and API semantic clarity
patterns.typescript: structural interfaces, branded IDs, async iterables for large results, Result errors, and adapter contract suites

patterns.name: Unit of Work
patterns.problem: multiple object changes in one business transaction must be tracked and committed consistently
patterns.exampleContext: an order-fulfillment use case modifying an order, inventory reservations, payment state, and audit records
patterns.mechanism: an explicit transactional context recording new, dirty, and removed objects and coordinating one commit or rollback
patterns.simplerAlternative: a database transaction around explicit SQL when change tracking adds no value
patterns.misuse: long-lived units, hidden global transaction state, nested transaction confusion, or mixing external calls inside database locks
patterns.evidence: transaction duration, partial-write defects, lock contention, rollback correctness, and dirty-tracking accuracy
patterns.typescript: AsyncLocalStorage hazards, explicit context parameters, typed repositories bound to a unit, and deterministic disposal

patterns.name: Identity Map
patterns.problem: the same database identity loaded repeatedly within one unit of work must refer to one in-memory object
patterns.exampleContext: a reservation workflow loading the same customer and inventory items through several repositories
patterns.mechanism: a scope-bound identity-to-object map that guarantees object identity and coordinates loading
patterns.simplerAlternative: immutable data snapshots when reference identity is irrelevant and merging is explicit
patterns.misuse: process-global maps, stale cross-request state, unbounded retention, tenant key collisions, or bypassing version checks
patterns.evidence: duplicate reads, identity conflicts, memory retention, scope leaks, and stale-object incidents
patterns.typescript: Map keys with branded IDs, explicit request scopes, WeakMap limitations, and unit-of-work ownership

patterns.name: Data Mapper
patterns.problem: domain objects and database representation must evolve independently
patterns.exampleContext: a clinical scheduling domain whose rich value objects and invariants do not match normalized relational tables
patterns.mechanism: dedicated bidirectional mapping between persistence records and domain objects without persistence behavior in the model
patterns.simplerAlternative: Active Record for simple row-shaped domains or direct SQL projections for read-only queries
patterns.misuse: mappers that bypass invariants, silent lossy conversion, reflection magic, or one enormous mapper for unrelated aggregates
patterns.evidence: mapping defects, domain persistence imports, query efficiency, schema migration impact, and round-trip invariants
patterns.typescript: schema decoders for unknown rows, branded identifiers, explicit null conversions, and compile-time mapped field checks

patterns.name: Active Record
patterns.problem: simple domain objects closely match database rows and benefit from colocated persistence operations
patterns.exampleContext: an internal catalog administration system dominated by validated CRUD and straightforward relationships
patterns.mechanism: objects representing rows expose focused persistence methods while retaining modest domain behavior
patterns.simplerAlternative: Data Mapper plus Repository when domain and persistence models diverge or testing isolation matters
patterns.misuse: using Active Record for complex aggregates, implicit queries from property access, shared mutable instances, or fat models owning everything
patterns.evidence: query transparency, test database dependency, coupling to schema, method growth, and transaction consistency
patterns.typescript: static factory typing, protected constructors, transaction parameters, runtime validation, and explicit async methods

patterns.name: Value Object
patterns.problem: a concept is defined by attributes and invariants rather than mutable identity
patterns.exampleContext: a commerce system representing money, currency, quantity, address, date range, percentage, and tax jurisdiction
patterns.mechanism: immutable values with validating construction, structural equality, domain operations, and explicit serialization
patterns.simplerAlternative: a branded primitive when the concept only needs validation and nominal distinction
patterns.misuse: mutable values, identity-based equality, invalid public constructors, primitive obsession inside the object, or excessive wrapper allocation
patterns.evidence: invalid value creation, equality defects, duplicated validation, allocation cost where material, and serialization fidelity
patterns.typescript: private constructors, readonly fields, factory Results, branded primitives, exact decimal libraries, and no floating-point money

patterns.name: Aggregate
patterns.problem: a cluster of domain objects needs one consistency boundary and one entry point for enforcing invariants
patterns.exampleContext: an inventory-reservation domain coordinating stock items, holds, expiration, and committed allocations
patterns.mechanism: an aggregate root protects invariants and controls changes inside a transaction-sized boundary
patterns.simplerAlternative: independent entities connected by identifiers and eventual consistency when one aggregate would become too large
patterns.misuse: loading an entire business graph, cross-aggregate object references, giant transactions, or treating every entity as an aggregate
patterns.evidence: aggregate load size, lock contention, transaction duration, invariant violations, and cross-boundary coordination events
patterns.typescript: private collections, readonly exposure, branded IDs, domain events, optimistic version fields, and repository-per-root

patterns.name: Specification
patterns.problem: business predicates must be named, composed, reused, tested, and sometimes translated to queries
patterns.exampleContext: a credit-eligibility engine combining jurisdiction, income, exposure, fraud, and product restrictions
patterns.mechanism: small domain predicates with explicit boolean composition and, where necessary, a separate translatable representation
patterns.simplerAlternative: plain predicate functions or decision tables when rules are local and composition remains readable
patterns.misuse: one class per trivial condition, leaking ORM expressions, combinator trees nobody can explain, or assuming all code predicates translate to SQL
patterns.evidence: rule duplication, explanation quality, query translation parity, evaluation cost, and branch coverage
patterns.typescript: predicate functions, discriminated expression trees, generic specifications, exhaustive translators, and explanation Results

patterns.name: Domain Event
patterns.problem: other parts of the domain need to react to a meaningful fact without the originating model coordinating every consequence
patterns.exampleContext: an insurance claims system reacting when a claim is submitted, assessed, approved, rejected, or paid
patterns.mechanism: immutable past-tense facts emitted by the domain and dispatched with explicitly chosen transactional semantics
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct calls for mandatory same-transaction invariants that must not be eventual
patterns.misuse: using events as commands, publishing before commit, vague names, payloads mirroring entire aggregates, or hidden synchronous chains
patterns.evidence: event usefulness, handler coupling, transaction consistency, duplicate handling, payload evolution, and causal traceability
patterns.typescript: readonly event unions, branded event IDs, occurred-at clocks, typed handler maps, and exhaustiveness

patterns.name: Anti-Corruption Layer
patterns.problem: a foreign model or legacy system would otherwise distort the application's domain language
patterns.exampleContext: a modern subscription platform integrating a legacy ERP whose customer, contract, invoice, and status concepts conflict
patterns.mechanism: a translation boundary with its own adapters, semantic mappings, error model, and vocabulary ownership
patterns.simplerAlternative: a simple Adapter when the mismatch is primarily syntactic rather than conceptual
patterns.misuse: a pass-through proxy, duplicated foreign concepts inside the domain, incomplete semantic mappings, or a second uncontrolled model
patterns.evidence: foreign-type imports, semantic translation defects, change containment, reconciliation failures, and mapping observability
patterns.typescript: separate packages, runtime schema validation, explicit mapping tables, Result errors, and no shared model types

patterns.name: CQRS
patterns.problem: read and write workloads have materially different models, scaling needs, permissions, or consistency expectations
patterns.exampleContext: a logistics platform with invariant-heavy shipment commands and high-volume operational tracking queries
patterns.mechanism: separate command and query models with explicit synchronization, ownership, and consistency contracts
patterns.simplerAlternative: one well-indexed relational model when asymmetry is small and operational simplicity dominates
patterns.misuse: splitting every CRUD service, claiming CQRS while sharing the same confused model, or hiding projection lag
patterns.evidence: write invariants, query latency, projection lag, operational components, schema duplication, and reconciliation burden
patterns.typescript: separate command/query contracts, discriminated messages, projection versioning, typed consistency metadata, and no shared mutable models

patterns.name: Event Sourcing
patterns.problem: the authoritative history of state changes must be retained and current state can be reconstructed from events
patterns.exampleContext: a regulated ledger tracking account decisions, corrections, reversals, and historical explanations
patterns.mechanism: append-only domain events as the source of truth, deterministic folds, snapshots, versioning, and controlled upcasting
patterns.simplerAlternative: audit logging beside ordinary state when full reconstruction and temporal queries are not required
patterns.misuse: treating database change logs as domain events, mutable events, side effects during replay, or ignoring schema evolution and deletion obligations
patterns.evidence: replay determinism, event volume, rebuild time, upcast coverage, storage growth, and projection correctness
patterns.typescript: readonly event unions, exhaustive folds, branded stream versions, schema validators, pure reducers, and bigint/decimal care

patterns.name: Data Transfer Object
patterns.problem: data must cross a process or layer boundary without exposing internal objects or causing excessive round trips
patterns.exampleContext: a public account API returning stable resources while internal domain and persistence models evolve
patterns.mechanism: purpose-specific serializable contracts assembled explicitly at the boundary
patterns.simplerAlternative: returning a narrow immutable value directly when it is already the intentional public contract
patterns.misuse: one universal DTO, exposing persistence rows, optional-field soup, versionless payloads, or mapping domain methods over the wire
patterns.evidence: contract churn, payload size, mapping defects, accidental data exposure, and backward compatibility
patterns.typescript: runtime schemas, `satisfies`, readonly serialized types, exact date/decimal representation, and versioned unions

patterns.name: Lazy Load
patterns.problem: related data is expensive and often unnecessary for the current use case
patterns.exampleContext: a content platform loading articles, revisions, authors, media, analytics, and permissions
patterns.mechanism: an explicit deferred reference, value holder, or query boundary that makes loading and failure visible
patterns.simplerAlternative: purpose-built queries or eager loading when access is predictable and round trips are cheaper than surprise
patterns.misuse: implicit property-triggered I/O, N+1 queries, access after transaction close, hidden network failure, or cache inconsistency
patterns.evidence: query count, latency distribution, unused data, access failure location, and transaction lifetime
patterns.typescript: explicit async loaders, memoized Promises with rejection policy, AbortSignal, Result errors, and no transparent getter I/O

patterns.name: Command Message
patterns.problem: one system must request that another perform a specific action asynchronously
patterns.exampleContext: an order platform sending reserve-inventory, capture-payment, and create-shipment requests
patterns.mechanism: an imperative message with one accountable consumer contract, stable intent, identity, and execution metadata
patterns.simplerAlternative: an Event Message when communicating a fact without prescribing the receiver's reaction
patterns.misuse: broadcasting commands, vague CRUD verbs, embedding implementation details, or retrying non-idempotent actions blindly
patterns.evidence: handler ownership, duplicate effects, command age, failure routing, and contract evolution
patterns.typescript: versioned discriminated message unions, branded command IDs, schema validation, and typed handler registries

patterns.name: Document Message
patterns.problem: systems need to transfer a self-contained data structure whose content matters more than the receiving action
patterns.exampleContext: a supplier integration distributing product catalogs and compliance documents
patterns.mechanism: a versioned document payload with explicit schema, ownership, completeness, and compatibility rules
patterns.simplerAlternative: an Event Message for temporal facts or a shared query API when receivers need fresh partial data
patterns.misuse: dumping internal database rows, unbounded documents, ambiguous partial updates, or schema changes without version strategy
patterns.evidence: payload size, schema compatibility, freshness, processing success, and semantic completeness
patterns.typescript: runtime decoders, versioned unions, readonly payloads, streaming parsers where needed, and explicit date/decimal encoding

patterns.name: Event Message
patterns.problem: systems need to announce that a meaningful fact occurred without directing a particular consumer
patterns.exampleContext: a marketplace announcing order-placed, payment-captured, item-shipped, and refund-issued facts
patterns.mechanism: an immutable past-tense message carrying identity, occurrence time, causation, correlation, and a minimal stable payload
patterns.simplerAlternative: a Command Message when one receiver is accountable for performing an action
patterns.misuse: events named after consumers, mutable facts, enormous snapshots, ambiguous ordering, or assuming publication means processing
patterns.evidence: consumer autonomy, duplicate safety, event age, schema evolution, causal tracing, and replay behavior
patterns.typescript: readonly versioned unions, branded IDs, schema validation, exact timestamps, and exhaustive consumers

patterns.name: Point-to-Point Channel
patterns.problem: each message must be processed by one eligible consumer rather than every subscriber
patterns.exampleContext: a media-processing queue distributing transcoding jobs among workers
patterns.mechanism: a queue with competing receivers, acknowledgment, redelivery, visibility, and dead-letter policies
patterns.simplerAlternative: Publish-Subscribe when every interested consumer needs its own copy
patterns.misuse: assuming ordering across workers, acknowledging before durable effects, infinite poison-message retries, or no backpressure
patterns.evidence: queue depth, age, redelivery, consumer utilization, poison messages, and processing latency
patterns.typescript: typed envelopes, abortable consumers, explicit ack outcomes, idempotency keys, and runtime payload validation

patterns.name: Publish-Subscribe Channel
patterns.problem: multiple independent consumers need copies of the same publication without sender knowledge
patterns.exampleContext: an account platform distributing account-opened events to analytics, risk, notifications, and CRM synchronization
patterns.mechanism: topic-based fan-out with per-subscriber delivery, retention, replay, and failure policy
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct calls for mandatory atomic work or Point-to-Point for one-of-many processing
patterns.misuse: confusing subscribers with load-balanced workers, losing offline consumers, uncontrolled fan-out, or shared subscription identities
patterns.evidence: subscriber lag, delivery completeness, fan-out cost, duplicate rates, retention, and failure isolation
patterns.typescript: typed topics, versioned event maps, independent consumer offsets, schema validation, and trace context

patterns.name: Request-Reply
patterns.problem: a requester needs a response while communication occurs over asynchronous messaging
patterns.exampleContext: a pricing gateway querying a remote risk engine through a broker with variable latency
patterns.mechanism: paired request and reply contracts connected through return address, correlation, timeout, and cancellation semantics
patterns.simplerAlternative: ordinary synchronous HTTP/RPC when broker decoupling adds no operational value
patterns.misuse: waiting forever, one reply queue per request, orphan replies, retrying ambiguous requests, or pretending the interaction is fire-and-forget
patterns.evidence: round-trip latency, timeout rate, orphan replies, broker resources, correlation correctness, and cancellation leakage
patterns.typescript: generic request/reply maps, branded correlation IDs, Promise cleanup, AbortSignal, and Result errors

patterns.name: Correlation Identifier
patterns.problem: responses and related messages must be associated with the originating request or workflow
patterns.exampleContext: a travel-booking workflow coordinating availability, reservation, payment, and ticket responses
patterns.mechanism: a stable correlation value propagated across message boundaries separately from message identity and causation
patterns.simplerAlternative: natural business keys only when uniqueness, privacy, and lifecycle semantics are truly sufficient
patterns.misuse: reusing message IDs as workflow IDs, regenerating IDs at boundaries, exposing sensitive identifiers, or missing trace propagation
patterns.evidence: uncorrelated messages, trace completeness, collision risk, workflow reconstruction, and privacy compliance
patterns.typescript: branded ID types, immutable envelopes, AsyncLocalStorage caution, typed metadata, and validation at ingress

patterns.name: Content-Based Router
patterns.problem: messages must be directed to destinations according to their content
patterns.exampleContext: a claims-ingestion service routing cases by jurisdiction, product, severity, and regulatory handling
patterns.mechanism: a deterministic routing decision separated from transport with explicit unmatched and multi-match behavior
patterns.simplerAlternative: separate producers or topic selection at the source when the source owns the routing fact cleanly
patterns.misuse: business rules buried in broker configuration, overlapping rules, silent drops, or routers mutating payloads
patterns.evidence: route coverage, unmatched rate, rule complexity, decision latency, and explainability
patterns.typescript: discriminated payloads, exhaustive decision tables, pure routing functions, schema validation, and typed destinations

patterns.name: Message Filter
patterns.problem: irrelevant or unwanted messages must be removed from a stream based on explicit criteria
patterns.exampleContext: a telemetry pipeline discarding unsupported, duplicate, expired, or policy-forbidden events
patterns.mechanism: a transparent predicate stage with observable accept, reject, and quarantine outcomes
patterns.simplerAlternative: consumer-side filtering when transport volume is small and consumer ownership is clearer
patterns.misuse: silent data loss, stateful filters without recovery, filtering before required audit, or confusing validation errors with irrelevance
patterns.evidence: accept/reject counts, false-positive rate, processing savings, audit completeness, and rule latency
patterns.typescript: type guards, predicate composition, Result-based validation, readonly messages, and explicit rejected-message types

patterns.name: Dynamic Router
patterns.problem: routing destinations change at runtime based on recipient capabilities, availability, or registrations
patterns.exampleContext: a document-conversion platform whose workers advertise supported formats and capacity
patterns.mechanism: a routing registry updated by controlled participant signals with expiration and fallback behavior
patterns.simplerAlternative: static configuration when destinations and capabilities change only at deployment time
patterns.misuse: trusting self-registration blindly, stale routes, oscillation, central registry bottlenecks, or no deterministic fallback
patterns.evidence: route freshness, failed dispatches, registry convergence, selection fairness, and fallback frequency
patterns.typescript: typed capability advertisements, expiry timestamps, readonly registry snapshots, Result selection, and concurrency-safe updates

patterns.name: Recipient List
patterns.problem: one message must be delivered to a dynamically determined set of recipients
patterns.exampleContext: a compliance system sending a case update to regulators, partners, and internal controls based on jurisdiction
patterns.mechanism: a deterministic recipient calculation followed by independently observable deliveries
patterns.simplerAlternative: Publish-Subscribe when the recipient set is subscriber-owned rather than sender-derived
patterns.misuse: duplicate destinations, partial delivery hidden as success, mutable recipient calculation, or exposing private recipient data
patterns.evidence: recipient accuracy, partial failures, duplicate deliveries, fan-out latency, and retry isolation
patterns.typescript: readonly recipient sets, branded destination IDs, Promise concurrency limits, Result aggregation, and typed policy rules

patterns.name: Splitter
patterns.problem: a composite message must be divided into independently processable parts
patterns.exampleContext: a bulk purchase order containing thousands of lines that need pricing, allocation, and fulfillment
patterns.mechanism: a split stage emitting parts with parent identity, sequence metadata, and completeness information
patterns.simplerAlternative: streaming the original document when independent routing and retry are unnecessary
patterns.misuse: losing parent context, unbounded fan-out, non-deterministic part identity, or acknowledging the parent before durable parts exist
patterns.evidence: fan-out size, split latency, missing parts, duplicate parts, backpressure, and parent completion accuracy
patterns.typescript: AsyncIterable, generators, branded parent/part IDs, readonly parts, and explicit sequence metadata

patterns.name: Aggregator
patterns.problem: related messages must be combined into one result despite partial arrival, duplication, delay, or failure
patterns.exampleContext: a travel search combining airline, hotel, rail, and insurance offers under a response deadline
patterns.mechanism: correlated state with completeness rules, timeout policy, duplicate handling, and a defined release condition
patterns.simplerAlternative: requesting one upstream facade when independent partial responses provide no value
patterns.misuse: waiting forever for completeness, unbounded state, double counting duplicates, ambiguous late arrivals, or no recovery after restart
patterns.evidence: completion rate, state size, timeout releases, late messages, duplicate suppression, and output correctness
patterns.typescript: typed correlation keys, reducer functions, durable state adapters, monotonic deadlines, and discriminated completion outcomes

patterns.name: Resequencer
patterns.problem: related messages arrive out of order but downstream processing requires an order
patterns.exampleContext: an account-event stream delivered across partitions where per-account sequence must be restored
patterns.mechanism: a bounded buffer keyed by sequence with gap detection, timeout, duplicate handling, and recovery
patterns.simplerAlternative: designing downstream behavior to tolerate reordering when strict order is unnecessary
patterns.misuse: global ordering, infinite waiting for missing messages, unbounded buffers, or trusting timestamps as exact sequence
patterns.evidence: buffer size, gap age, late arrivals, duplicate rate, release latency, and partition-local correctness
patterns.typescript: branded sequence numbers, ordered maps, bigint where needed, discriminated gap outcomes, and durable checkpoints

patterns.name: Message Translator
patterns.problem: two messaging participants use different data formats or semantic models
patterns.exampleContext: a healthcare integration converting partner claims into the platform's canonical claim events
patterns.mechanism: an explicit, versioned translation step with validation, semantic mapping, error quarantine, and provenance
patterns.simplerAlternative: Adapter inside one process or Anti-Corruption Layer for a broader conceptual boundary
patterns.misuse: field-copy mapping without semantic analysis, silent defaulting, lossy round trips, or mixing routing with translation
patterns.evidence: mapping failures, quarantined volume, semantic reconciliation, version coverage, and provenance retention
patterns.typescript: runtime schemas, exhaustive source-version unions, Result errors, branded units, and pure mapping functions

patterns.name: Canonical Data Model
patterns.problem: many systems would otherwise require pairwise translations between every representation
patterns.exampleContext: an organization integrating commerce, ERP, warehouse, billing, support, and analytics systems
patterns.mechanism: a deliberately governed integration model with versioning and translators at system boundaries
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct pairwise translation for a small stable topology where a shared model would create more coordination
patterns.misuse: an enterprise-wide god schema, lowest-common-denominator semantics, centralized release blocking, or domain ownership erosion
patterns.evidence: translator count, schema churn, governance lead time, semantic loss, and team coupling
patterns.typescript: versioned schema packages, readonly DTOs, compatibility tests, namespaced unions, and runtime decoding

patterns.name: Idempotent Receiver
patterns.problem: at-least-once delivery means the same message may be processed more than once
patterns.exampleContext: a payment-settlement consumer receiving redelivered capture and refund messages
patterns.mechanism: stable message identity plus atomic duplicate detection and effect recording at the receiver's consistency boundary
patterns.simplerAlternative: naturally idempotent state assignment when the business operation genuinely has identical repeated effects
patterns.misuse: check-then-act races, in-memory deduplication, expiring keys too early, or using correlation IDs instead of unique message IDs
patterns.evidence: duplicate side effects, dedupe hit rate, storage growth, race tests, and replay correctness
patterns.typescript: branded message IDs, database unique constraints, transaction-scoped Results, and deterministic handler contracts

patterns.name: Transactional Outbox
patterns.problem: a database change and message publication must not diverge despite crashes between two independent systems
patterns.exampleContext: an order service that must persist an accepted order and eventually publish OrderPlaced
patterns.mechanism: business state and an outbox record committed atomically, followed by asynchronous relay and idempotent consumption
patterns.simplerAlternative: database-native change streams when their operational and semantic guarantees fit the domain
patterns.misuse: publishing inside the transaction, deleting before broker acknowledgment, no ordering key, or treating relay duplicates as impossible
patterns.evidence: lost events, relay lag, duplicate publications, outbox growth, transaction overhead, and recovery time
patterns.typescript: typed outbox envelopes, JSON schema validation, branded sequence IDs, explicit relay states, and database transactions

patterns.name: Competing Consumers
patterns.problem: a queue-backed workload must scale horizontally while each message is processed by only one worker
patterns.exampleContext: a report-generation service absorbing bursty jobs with widely varying execution cost
patterns.mechanism: multiple equivalent consumers share a point-to-point channel with controlled concurrency and idempotent processing
patterns.simplerAlternative: partitioned consumers when key ordering or state affinity matters
patterns.misuse: unbounded consumer concurrency, hot-key starvation, assuming perfect fairness, or autoscaling only on CPU
patterns.evidence: queue age, throughput, utilization, redelivery, fairness, saturation, and cost per completed job
patterns.typescript: worker pools, AbortSignal, bounded Promise concurrency, typed acknowledgments, and process-level isolation

patterns.name: Timeout
patterns.problem: a remote or asynchronous operation can wait indefinitely and consume bounded resources
patterns.exampleContext: a checkout aggregator calling inventory, pricing, fraud, loyalty, and payment services
patterns.mechanism: an explicit deadline propagated across calls with cancellation, cleanup, and a domain-aware timeout outcome
patterns.simplerAlternative: no timeout only for bounded in-process computation whose completion is guaranteed by construction
patterns.misuse: stacking independent timeouts that exceed the caller deadline, abandoning work without cancellation, or retrying every timeout
patterns.evidence: timeout rate, wasted work, resource occupancy, deadline propagation, p99 latency, and cleanup latency
patterns.typescript: AbortController, AbortSignal composition, typed timeout errors, monotonic timing, and Promise cleanup

patterns.name: Retry with Backoff and Jitter
patterns.problem: a transient failure may succeed later, but immediate synchronized retries amplify overload
patterns.exampleContext: a webhook delivery service handling rate limits, network errors, and intermittent partner outages
patterns.mechanism: classified retryable failures, bounded attempts, exponential backoff, jitter, deadlines, and idempotency
patterns.simplerAlternative: fail fast for permanent failures or queue for operator-mediated repair when automated retry is unsafe
patterns.misuse: retrying non-idempotent operations, retrying overload, nested retry storms, ignoring Retry-After, or resetting attempt history
patterns.evidence: attempt distribution, success-after-retry, added latency, amplification factor, duplicate effects, and exhausted retries
patterns.typescript: typed error classification, AbortSignal, injected clock/randomness, bigint-safe delays, and explicit attempt context

patterns.name: Circuit Breaker
patterns.problem: calls to a failing dependency waste resources and prolong recovery
patterns.exampleContext: a recommendation API depending on a personalization service that sometimes becomes slow or unavailable
patterns.mechanism: a state machine that opens after meaningful failure evidence, probes in half-open state, and closes after recovery
patterns.simplerAlternative: rate limiting or admission control when the problem is caller overload rather than dependency health
patterns.misuse: one global breaker for unrelated operations, counting business rejections as faults, fixed windows without traffic context, or no observability
patterns.evidence: breaker state time, rejected calls, probe success, recovery time, false openings, and downstream load reduction
patterns.typescript: discriminated state, monotonic clock, atomic updates, typed failure classification, and per-operation registries

patterns.name: Bulkhead
patterns.problem: failure or saturation in one workload must not consume all shared resources
patterns.exampleContext: a multi-tenant document platform where large exports can starve interactive requests
patterns.mechanism: separate resource pools, queues, concurrency budgets, or processes aligned with failure domains
patterns.simplerAlternative: priority scheduling in one pool when rigid partitioning would waste scarce capacity
patterns.misuse: arbitrary partitions, no overflow policy, bulkheads sharing the real bottleneck, or static limits without measurement
patterns.evidence: cross-workload latency, pool saturation, rejected work, utilization, recovery isolation, and reserved capacity cost
patterns.typescript: bounded worker pools, semaphores, AbortSignal, per-tenant maps with eviction, and typed admission outcomes

patterns.name: Rate Limiter
patterns.problem: demand must be admitted at a controlled rate to protect capacity, fairness, quotas, or external contracts
patterns.exampleContext: a public inference API enforcing tenant quotas while protecting GPU-backed workers
patterns.mechanism: a documented token-bucket, leaky-bucket, fixed-window, or sliding-window policy with explicit scope and rejection metadata
patterns.simplerAlternative: backpressure or bounded queues when callers can wait and work should not be discarded
patterns.misuse: per-process limits in a distributed deployment, wall-clock bugs, unfair shared buckets, unlimited cardinality, or hiding overload as timeouts
patterns.evidence: admitted/rejected rate, fairness, burst behavior, limiter-state cardinality, latency, and downstream saturation
patterns.typescript: monotonic clocks, bigint token arithmetic, atomic storage operations, branded tenant keys, and typed Retry-After

patterns.name: Cache-Aside
patterns.problem: frequently read data is expensive to obtain and can tolerate an explicit freshness policy
patterns.exampleContext: a product API serving catalog and availability data from PostgreSQL under heavy read traffic
patterns.mechanism: application-controlled lookup, population, invalidation, expiry, and stampede protection around a source of truth
patterns.simplerAlternative: database indexes, materialized views, or request-local memoization when a distributed cache is unjustified
patterns.misuse: unbounded keys, caching errors, stale authorization, cache stampedes, ambiguous null caching, or dual writes
patterns.evidence: hit rate, source load, staleness, memory, eviction, stampede concurrency, and p95/p99 latency
patterns.typescript: generic cache ports, branded keys, TTL types, Promise coalescing, Result-aware negative caching, and serialization schemas

patterns.name: Leader Election
patterns.problem: one participant among peers must temporarily coordinate a singleton responsibility
patterns.exampleContext: a scheduler cluster that should emit each periodic billing job from one active coordinator
patterns.mechanism: a consensus-backed or lease-backed election with fencing, explicit terms, and safe handover
patterns.simplerAlternative: partitioning work deterministically so no leader is required
patterns.misuse: assuming election prevents split brain, acting without fencing tokens, long unrenewed leadership, or coupling all progress to one leader
patterns.evidence: election time, dual-leader incidents, availability during handover, term changes, and fenced-write rejection
patterns.typescript: branded term/fencing tokens, monotonic lease handling, explicit state unions, and abortable leadership tasks

patterns.name: Lease
patterns.problem: exclusive ownership must expire automatically when a holder crashes or loses connectivity
patterns.exampleContext: a distributed worker claiming long-running media jobs with recoverable ownership
patterns.mechanism: time-bounded ownership renewed by the holder and protected by fencing or version checks
patterns.simplerAlternative: a short atomic transaction when work completes inside one storage operation
patterns.misuse: using wall clocks without skew analysis, renewing after expiry, no fencing, lease duration shorter than worst pauses, or silent ownership loss
patterns.evidence: expired work, duplicate ownership, renewal latency, takeover time, fenced operations, and clock sensitivity
patterns.typescript: branded lease IDs, monotonic local timers, versioned compare-and-swap, AbortSignal on loss, and explicit expiry states

patterns.name: Saga
patterns.problem: a business transaction spans autonomous services that cannot share one atomic database transaction
patterns.exampleContext: a travel-booking workflow reserving flight, hotel, payment, insurance, and loyalty benefits
patterns.mechanism: a sequence of local transactions with persisted progress, compensations, timeouts, idempotency, and either orchestration or choreography
patterns.simplerAlternative: one local transaction in a modular monolith when distribution is not required
patterns.misuse: treating compensation as rollback, undocumented irreversibility, event choreography with no owner, or no manual recovery path
patterns.evidence: completion time, compensation rate, stuck instances, duplicate actions, manual interventions, and business residuals
patterns.typescript: versioned saga state unions, typed commands/events, persistent steps, branded correlation IDs, and exhaustive recovery transitions

patterns.name: Strangler Fig
patterns.problem: a legacy system must be replaced incrementally without a high-risk big-bang rewrite
patterns.exampleContext: a monolithic insurance platform being decomposed by customer-facing capabilities
patterns.mechanism: a routing seam sends selected capabilities to new implementations while migration, parity, and retirement are measured
patterns.simplerAlternative: in-place modular refactoring when deployment separation provides no real benefit
patterns.misuse: a permanent proxy layer, duplicating writes indefinitely, migrating by technical layer, or no deletion criteria for legacy paths
patterns.evidence: traffic migrated, behavioral parity, defect rate, dual-run cost, dependency reduction, and retired code
patterns.typescript: typed boundary contracts, shadow comparison, feature flags, schema adapters, and explicit route ownership

patterns.name: API Gateway
patterns.problem: external clients need one governed entry point to multiple backend capabilities
patterns.exampleContext: a commerce platform exposing authentication, routing, quotas, aggregation, and protocol translation
patterns.mechanism: an edge boundary handling cross-cutting transport concerns while domain logic remains in services
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct service exposure for trusted internal traffic with adequate service-level controls
patterns.misuse: business logic in the gateway, one gateway for incompatible audiences, a scaling bottleneck, or hiding service failures
patterns.evidence: gateway latency, route availability, policy consistency, coupling to services, and blast radius
patterns.typescript: typed route contracts, schema validation, AbortSignal deadlines, streaming, and generated clients without shared domain types

patterns.name: Backend for Frontend
patterns.problem: different client experiences need distinct aggregation, payload, latency, and release decisions
patterns.exampleContext: a platform serving browser IDE, mobile progress view, CLI, and administrative console
patterns.mechanism: a thin client-specific backend owning presentation-oriented orchestration and contracts
patterns.simplerAlternative: one general API when clients truly share needs and duplication would dominate
patterns.misuse: duplicating domain logic, one BFF per screen, tightly coupling teams, or turning BFFs into uncontrolled data silos
patterns.evidence: payload efficiency, client round trips, duplicated logic, independent deployment value, and end-to-end latency
patterns.typescript: client-specific DTOs, schema-generated clients, streaming responses, Result aggregation, and no shared mutable model

patterns.name: Sidecar
patterns.problem: a workload needs adjacent operational capabilities that should remain separately deployable
patterns.exampleContext: a service requiring local telemetry forwarding, certificate rotation, and protocol translation
patterns.mechanism: a companion process sharing a lifecycle and selected resources with the primary workload
patterns.simplerAlternative: an in-process library when latency, simplicity, and shared failure are acceptable
patterns.misuse: one sidecar per fashionable concern, hidden resource doubling, startup races, version drift, or security boundary confusion
patterns.evidence: resource overhead, startup ordering, failure coupling, network hops, rollout consistency, and operational ownership
patterns.typescript: typed local protocols, health contracts, AbortSignal shutdown, Unix-socket clients, and version negotiation

patterns.name: Ambassador
patterns.problem: a workload needs a local proxy for outbound connectivity concerns such as discovery, retries, routing, or credentials
patterns.exampleContext: a legacy service connecting securely to modern external APIs through a local companion
patterns.mechanism: an out-of-process outbound proxy presenting a simple local endpoint while centralizing transport policy
patterns.simplerAlternative: an Adapter library when the application can safely own and update the integration
patterns.misuse: hiding remote semantics, duplicate retry policies, proxy becoming a privileged bottleneck, or unclear telemetry attribution
patterns.evidence: connection success, added latency, policy consistency, credential exposure, and retry amplification
patterns.typescript: typed local client contracts, explicit deadlines, trace propagation, Unix sockets, and Result errors

patterns.name: Sharding
patterns.problem: one data or workload partition cannot meet scale, locality, or isolation requirements
patterns.exampleContext: a multi-tenant event store exceeding one PostgreSQL cluster's write and storage capacity
patterns.mechanism: a stable shard key, routing layer, metadata ownership, rebalancing process, and cross-shard constraint policy
patterns.simplerAlternative: vertical scaling, table partitioning, read replicas, or archival before accepting distributed complexity
patterns.misuse: hot shards, mutable shard keys, cross-shard transactions everywhere, routing metadata split brain, or no rebalancing plan
patterns.evidence: key distribution, hottest-shard saturation, cross-shard query rate, rebalance cost, and tenant isolation
patterns.typescript: branded shard keys, pure routing functions, consistent-hash evaluation, typed metadata versions, and exhaustive routing failures

patterns.name: Materialized View
patterns.problem: queries need a precomputed representation different from the authoritative write model
patterns.exampleContext: an operations dashboard requiring real-time counts, latency summaries, and learner competency projections
patterns.mechanism: a derived read model maintained synchronously or asynchronously with rebuild and reconciliation capability
patterns.simplerAlternative: indexes or direct queries when the source model can meet the latency and scale objective
patterns.misuse: treating the view as authoritative, no rebuild path, hidden lag, non-idempotent updates, or uncontrolled view proliferation
patterns.evidence: query latency, projection lag, rebuild time, divergence, storage cost, and update throughput
patterns.typescript: typed projection events, pure reducers, versioned checkpoints, idempotent writes, and explicit consistency metadata

patterns.name: Eventual Consistency
patterns.problem: autonomous components cannot or should not make every state change atomically visible everywhere
patterns.exampleContext: a marketplace where inventory, search, recommendations, analytics, and notifications update at different times
patterns.mechanism: an explicit convergence model with monotonic progress, conflict policy, freshness communication, and repair
patterns.simplerAlternative: strong consistency within one aggregate or database when latency and availability requirements permit it
patterns.misuse: using eventual consistency as an excuse for missing invariants, no user-visible pending state, last-write-wins by accident, or no reconciliation
patterns.evidence: convergence time, stale-read rate, conflict frequency, repair backlog, user-visible anomalies, and invariant residuals
patterns.typescript: version vectors or sequence metadata where justified, state unions exposing pending status, idempotent reducers, and typed conflict outcomes

patterns.name: Singleflight
patterns.problem: concurrent identical requests trigger duplicate concurrent executions of the same expensive downstream work or cache fill
patterns.exampleContext: a high-traffic news platform where hundreds of concurrent requests for a breaking article all miss the cache at the same millisecond
patterns.mechanism: in-flight request coalescing using an in-memory key map that multiplexes all duplicate concurrent callers onto a single shared execution Promise
patterns.simplerAlternative: simple mutex locking or allowing duplicate reads when downstream workload is cheap and concurrency is low
patterns.misuse: retaining completed promises causing memory leaks, sharing errors unconditionally without retry context, holding long timeouts across all waiters, or applying to mutating operations
patterns.evidence: duplicate downstream call suppression ratio, origin load under cache misses, waiter latency distribution, in-flight map cardinality, and memory occupancy
patterns.typescript: generic Promise sharing, key-based flight registry, `finally` cleanup, error propagation, AbortSignal coordination, and typed return values

patterns.name: Cache-Aside Stampede Lock
patterns.problem: cache expiration of a hot key causes massive concurrent backend requests (thundering herd or stampede) that overwhelm the source database
patterns.exampleContext: a flash-sale product catalog cache expiring during peak traffic causing thousands of concurrent database queries for the same product
patterns.mechanism: a distributed mutex lock acquired with lease TTL by only one worker to regenerate the cache while other callers back off, retry, or serve stale data
patterns.simplerAlternative: singleflight for single-process coalescing, probabilistic early expiration (XFetch), or background pre-warming
patterns.misuse: lock starvation without fallback, long lock timeouts blocking readers, deadlocks on unreleased locks, missing lease renewals for slow regeneration, or herd on lock polling
patterns.evidence: database peak read QPS during cache expiration, stampede lock contention rate, stale-hit ratio, p99 latency during invalidation, and lock acquisition timeout frequency
patterns.typescript: distributed lease tokens, atomic Redis/KV primitives, exponential jittered backoff loops, stale-while-revalidate schemas, and typed lock guards

patterns.name: Mutex
patterns.problem: multiple concurrent actors must not enter a critical section simultaneously
patterns.exampleContext: a Node.js worker coordinating asynchronous updates to a shared in-memory index and file-backed checkpoint
patterns.mechanism: exclusive ownership with minimal critical sections, defined acquisition order, cancellation, and guaranteed release
