patterns.simplerAlternative: atomic database operations, immutable data, message passing, or partitioned ownership that removes sharing
patterns.misuse: assuming the event loop prevents races, awaiting arbitrary I/O while locked, lock-order cycles, or process-local locks for distributed state
patterns.evidence: wait time, hold time, contention, deadlocks, throughput, and correctness under deterministic interleavings
patterns.typescript: Promise-based mutexes, `try/finally`, AbortSignal, worker boundaries, and explicit process-scope limitations

patterns.name: Semaphore
patterns.problem: a limited resource allows some concurrency but must not be oversubscribed
patterns.exampleContext: an ingestion service limiting simultaneous database imports and external API calls
patterns.mechanism: a counted permit pool with bounded waiting, cancellation, fairness policy, and guaranteed release
patterns.simplerAlternative: a queue or rate limiter when scheduling order or time-based admission is the primary concern
patterns.misuse: permit leaks, acquiring multiple semaphores in inconsistent order, unlimited waiters, or confusing concurrency with rate
patterns.evidence: permit utilization, queue time, waiters, fairness, resource saturation, and timeout rate
patterns.typescript: typed permit handles, `using`/disposal where supported, `try/finally`, AbortSignal, and bounded Promise pools

patterns.name: Producer-Consumer
patterns.problem: work production and processing proceed at different rates and require buffering and coordination
patterns.exampleContext: a source-code analyzer streaming files to parse, metric, dependency, and report workers
patterns.mechanism: a bounded queue decoupling producers and consumers with backpressure, completion, failure, and shutdown semantics
patterns.simplerAlternative: a direct pipeline when each stage naturally awaits the next and buffering adds no throughput
patterns.misuse: unbounded queues, lost shutdown signals, poison work blocking progress, or producers ignoring backpressure
patterns.evidence: queue depth, age, throughput, saturation, dropped work, shutdown completeness, and memory
patterns.typescript: AsyncIterable, bounded channels, AbortSignal, discriminated work results, worker threads, and transferable objects

patterns.name: Reader-Writer Lock
patterns.problem: many readers can proceed together but writes require exclusive access
patterns.exampleContext: a runtime configuration registry with frequent reads and occasional atomic reloads
patterns.mechanism: separate shared-read and exclusive-write acquisition with an explicit fairness and upgrade policy
patterns.simplerAlternative: immutable snapshot replacement when readers can cheaply share a versioned value
patterns.misuse: writer starvation, lock upgrade deadlock, holding read locks across I/O, or using process-local locks for shared database data
patterns.evidence: read throughput, writer wait, starvation, hold time, snapshot alternative cost, and consistency defects
patterns.typescript: Promise-based locks, immutable snapshots, AbortSignal, atomics in worker scenarios, and no false distributed guarantees

patterns.name: Actor
patterns.problem: independent stateful components need concurrency without sharing mutable state
patterns.exampleContext: a multiplayer collaboration service managing one document session per actor
patterns.mechanism: isolated state owned by an actor that processes one mailbox message at a time and communicates only through messages
patterns.simplerAlternative: a plain object behind one request handler when concurrency and lifecycle isolation are absent
patterns.misuse: unbounded mailboxes, blocking actor handlers, distributed-location transparency, no supervision, or chatty actor graphs
patterns.evidence: mailbox age, processing latency, actor count, restarts, message amplification, and state isolation
patterns.typescript: typed message unions, exhaustive receive functions, worker threads or processes, supervision Results, and serialization boundaries

patterns.name: Reactor
patterns.problem: many I/O events must be demultiplexed and dispatched efficiently without one blocking thread per connection
patterns.exampleContext: a high-concurrency gateway handling sockets, timers, streaming bodies, and backpressure
patterns.mechanism: an event loop waits for readiness and dispatches short non-blocking handlers while long work moves elsewhere
patterns.simplerAlternative: thread or worker-per-task models when CPU-bound isolation and simpler blocking code are more important
patterns.misuse: blocking the event loop, recursive event storms, ignoring backpressure, or assuming callback completion ordering
patterns.evidence: event-loop delay, handler duration, connection count, throughput, memory per connection, and backpressure
patterns.typescript: Bun/Node event-loop semantics, streams, AsyncIterable, AbortSignal, worker threads, and no synchronous CPU spikes

patterns.name: Promise/Future
patterns.problem: a computation result will become available later and consumers need a composable handle now
patterns.exampleContext: a build orchestrator running dependency-aware compilation, tests, and artifact analysis
patterns.mechanism: a single-assignment eventual result supporting composition, failure propagation, and coordinated waiting
patterns.simplerAlternative: callbacks or events when multiple values, cancellation streams, or repeated notifications are fundamental
patterns.misuse: floating promises, lost rejection causes, sequential awaits of independent work, uncontrolled `Promise.all`, or pretending cancellation exists
patterns.evidence: critical path duration, concurrency, unhandled rejections, abandoned work, memory retention, and failure causality
patterns.typescript: Promise combinators, typed Results, AbortSignal, `Awaited`, concurrency bounds, and explicit task ownership

patterns.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
patterns.problem: concurrent updates are uncommon enough that conflicts can be detected rather than prevented by long locks
patterns.exampleContext: an inventory and document-editing API updating versioned records
patterns.mechanism: read a version, attempt a conditional write, and resolve or retry explicit conflicts
patterns.simplerAlternative: pessimistic locking when contention is high and conflict work is expensive or unsafe to repeat
patterns.misuse: unbounded retries, merging non-commutative changes blindly, missing version checks on side tables, or returning generic server errors
patterns.evidence: conflict rate, retries, lost updates, user resolution, contention crossover, and transaction duration
patterns.typescript: branded version numbers, discriminated conflict Results, conditional SQL, pure merge functions, and bounded retry

patterns.name: Token Bucket Rate Limiter
patterns.problem: traffic streams require a bounded consumption rate while accommodating legitimate short-duration bursts without dropping requests
patterns.exampleContext: a payment or file upload processing queue that permits short bursts of 20 concurrent tasks but enforces a sustained limit of 5 tasks per second
patterns.mechanism: a token bucket with maximum capacity that continuously refills at a fixed rate, allowing immediate admission when tokens exist and delaying or rejecting when empty
patterns.simplerAlternative: fixed window or sliding window counter when burst tolerance is unnecessary, or simple semaphore for pure concurrency limits
patterns.misuse: clock skew in distributed multi-node token generation, excessive token lock contention, uncalibrated bucket capacity causing downstream starvation, or unobserved drop rates
patterns.evidence: burst admission success rate, token refill latency, rejected request volume, sustained throughput stability, downstream queue depth, and burst duration metrics
patterns.typescript: monotonic timestamp math, floating refill arithmetic, atomic token consumption, typed delay scheduling, and rate limit error contracts

patterns.name: Test Double
patterns.problem: a collaborator must be controlled or observed during a test without using the real dependency
patterns.exampleContext: an order workflow depending on a clock, payment gateway, queue, repository, and notification service
patterns.mechanism: purposeful stubs, spies, fakes, mocks, or dummies selected according to the test's actual observation need
patterns.simplerAlternative: the real component in an integration or contract test when substitution would hide the important risk
patterns.misuse: mocking every internal call, brittle interaction assertions, dishonest fakes, or using one word for all double types
patterns.evidence: test brittleness, false confidence, setup size, contract parity, mutation score, and meaningful failure messages
patterns.typescript: structural ports, typed fake builders, readonly call records, `satisfies`, and minimal capability interfaces

patterns.name: Test Data Builder
patterns.problem: tests need valid, expressive variations of complex data without copying enormous fixtures
patterns.exampleContext: a subscription domain whose plans, accounts, invoices, taxes, and dates have many invariants
patterns.mechanism: a builder provides sensible valid defaults and named overrides while preserving the reason each test differs
patterns.simplerAlternative: literal object creation for small values or domain factories when tests should use the same public construction path
patterns.misuse: one universal builder, hidden invalid defaults, fluent noise, shared mutable state, or tests overriding unrelated fields
patterns.evidence: fixture duplication, setup-to-assertion ratio, invalid test data, change amplification, and readability
patterns.typescript: readonly defaults, Partial overrides with validation, branded values, factory functions, and no unsafe casts

patterns.name: Humble Object
patterns.problem: hard-to-test framework, UI, clock, process, or infrastructure code contains important logic
patterns.exampleContext: a WebSocket session handler combining protocol events, timers, reconnection, and state decisions
patterns.mechanism: keep the boundary object deliberately simple and move decisions into deterministic collaborators
patterns.simplerAlternative: an end-to-end test when the boundary behavior itself is the primary risk
patterns.misuse: a useless pass-through layer, moving framework types into the core, or declaring all integration code unworthy of tests
patterns.evidence: core mutation score, boundary complexity, end-to-end test count, deterministic coverage, and defect localization
patterns.typescript: Functional Core Imperative Shell, typed adapters, injected clocks, state reducers, and schema-decoded events

patterns.name: Characterization Test
patterns.problem: existing behavior must be captured before safely changing poorly understood code
patterns.exampleContext: a legacy pricing engine with undocumented rounding, exceptions, fallbacks, and customer-specific branches
patterns.mechanism: observation-focused tests record current externally visible behavior, including surprising cases, before refactoring
patterns.simplerAlternative: specification tests when intended behavior is already known and current defects must not be preserved
patterns.misuse: asserting incidental internals, snapshotting huge unstable outputs, calling every current behavior correct, or stopping after capture
patterns.evidence: behavior surface captured, refactoring regressions, brittle assertions, newly identified defects, and mutation score
patterns.typescript: Vitest parameterization, deterministic seams, fake clocks, explicit unknown behavior notes, and narrow snapshots

patterns.name: Contract Test
patterns.problem: independently developed consumers and providers must agree on observable interaction semantics
patterns.exampleContext: a platform with several carrier adapters and externally deployed clients
patterns.mechanism: a shared or consumer-driven executable contract run against every implementation at the boundary
patterns.simplerAlternative: integration tests against one deployment when version independence and substitution are irrelevant
patterns.misuse: testing only types, provider states that cannot be reproduced, contracts mirroring implementation, or ignoring non-functional semantics
patterns.evidence: compatibility failures, adapter parity, contract coverage, provider-state reproducibility, and version adoption time
patterns.typescript: runtime schemas, generic contract suites, `satisfies`, typed fixtures, and transport-independent assertions

patterns.name: Property-Based Testing
patterns.problem: behavior is better described by general invariants than by a handful of chosen examples
patterns.exampleContext: a money allocation and event-folding library with large combinatorial input spaces
patterns.mechanism: generators produce diverse inputs while invariant properties and shrinking expose minimal counterexamples
patterns.simplerAlternative: example tests for named business cases whose meaning would be obscured by generators
patterns.misuse: tautological properties, invalid generators, enormous slow domains, nondeterministic seeds, or replacing all examples
patterns.evidence: counterexamples found, shrink quality, generator validity, execution budget, mutation score, and invariant coverage
patterns.typescript: fast-check arbitraries, branded-value generators, Result-aware properties, deterministic seeds, and exhaustive small domains

patterns.name: Approval Testing
patterns.problem: complex output is easier to review as a whole than to assert field by field
patterns.exampleContext: a compiler producing query plans, formatted diagnostics, and architecture reports
patterns.mechanism: a deliberately reviewed approved artifact compared against normalized current output
patterns.simplerAlternative: focused assertions when only a small stable contract matters
patterns.misuse: rubber-stamping diffs, snapshots full of timestamps and IDs, gigantic fixtures, or approving defects without investigation
patterns.evidence: reviewed diff size, snapshot churn, defect detection, normalization complexity, and diagnostic quality
patterns.typescript: Vitest snapshots or explicit golden files, deterministic serialization, stable ordering, redaction, and narrow approval scopes

patterns.name: Mutation Testing
patterns.problem: passing tests may execute code without detecting meaningful behavioral changes
patterns.exampleContext: a rules and pricing engine with apparently high line coverage but recurring escaped defects
patterns.mechanism: systematic code mutations measure whether the suite kills plausible faults and reveal weak assertions
patterns.simplerAlternative: targeted manual fault injection for unsupported tooling or very small critical algorithms
patterns.misuse: treating mutation score as a universal target, testing equivalent mutants forever, mutating generated code, or ignoring runtime cost
patterns.evidence: mutation score by risk area, surviving mutants, execution time, flaky results, and assertion improvements
patterns.typescript: StrykerJS, selective mutators, Vitest integration, incremental scope, and documented equivalent mutants

patterns.name: Layered Architecture
patterns.problem: a system needs separation by responsibility and controlled dependency direction
patterns.exampleContext: a business application separating delivery, application, domain, and infrastructure concerns
patterns.mechanism: logical layers with explicit responsibilities, dependency rules, and intentional bypass policy
patterns.simplerAlternative: vertical feature slices when technical layers cause excessive cross-folder scattering
patterns.misuse: pass-through layers, cyclic dependencies, domain depending on delivery, or treating folders as architecture enforcement
patterns.evidence: dependency violations, change spread, pass-through count, build boundaries, and test isolation
patterns.typescript: TypeScript project references, package exports, dependency-cruiser rules, type-only imports, and separate contracts

patterns.name: Ports and Adapters
patterns.problem: core application behavior must remain independent of delivery mechanisms and infrastructure providers
patterns.exampleContext: a billing platform used through HTTP, CLI, jobs, and messages with PostgreSQL and external payment providers
patterns.mechanism: inbound and outbound ports define capabilities around an application core while adapters handle technologies
patterns.simplerAlternative: a simple layered module when infrastructure variation and domain isolation do not justify extra boundaries
patterns.misuse: one interface per class, domain ports shaped like database APIs, adapter leakage, or symmetric diagrams hiding asymmetric policy
patterns.evidence: core infrastructure imports, adapter contract parity, test setup, replacement effort, and boundary semantic quality
patterns.typescript: structural ports, package export maps, composition root, runtime schemas, dependency-cruiser, and Result errors

patterns.name: Modular Monolith
patterns.problem: a system needs strong capability boundaries and team-scale modularity without distributed deployment costs
patterns.exampleContext: a growing learning platform containing identity, catalog, lab execution, assessment, billing, and analytics
patterns.mechanism: one deployable with independently owned modules, private data, explicit contracts, and enforced dependency direction
patterns.simplerAlternative: microservices when capabilities require independent scaling, failure isolation, deployment, or regulatory ownership
patterns.misuse: folders called modules with shared tables and imports everywhere, distributed-style internal HTTP, or one global domain model
patterns.evidence: cross-module dependencies, private-table violations, build coupling, deployment frequency, transaction clarity, and extraction readiness
patterns.typescript: workspace packages, export maps, project references, architecture tests, module-owned schemas, and in-process typed messages

patterns.name: Microkernel
patterns.problem: a stable core must support independently developed or selected extensions
patterns.exampleContext: a code-analysis platform loading metric, language, report, and evaluator plugins
patterns.mechanism: a minimal kernel owns lifecycle and contracts while plugins register bounded capabilities through versioned interfaces
patterns.simplerAlternative: compile-time composition when extension sets are controlled and dynamic loading provides no benefit
patterns.misuse: an omniscient kernel, plugins importing internals, no compatibility negotiation, unsafe third-party code, or dependency conflicts
patterns.evidence: kernel stability, plugin isolation, startup time, compatibility failures, extension effort, and security surface
patterns.typescript: dynamic import, versioned structural contracts, runtime validation, isolated workers, capability permissions, and package exports

patterns.name: Pipes and Filters
patterns.problem: processing can be decomposed into reusable stages connected by data flow
patterns.exampleContext: a source-analysis pipeline performing discovery, parsing, normalization, metrics, graph building, and reporting
patterns.mechanism: independent filters with explicit input/output contracts connected by pipes with backpressure and error semantics
patterns.simplerAlternative: one cohesive function when stages do not vary, reuse, or operate independently
patterns.misuse: chatty tiny filters, materializing every intermediate, mismatched schemas, no backpressure, or hiding global state in stages
patterns.evidence: stage throughput, queue depth, memory, parallelism, failure localization, reuse, and end-to-end latency
patterns.typescript: AsyncIterable, generators, Web Streams, runtime schemas, Result channels, AbortSignal, and worker boundaries

patterns.name: Event-Driven Architecture
patterns.problem: components need temporal decoupling and reaction to facts across independent lifecycles
patterns.exampleContext: a commerce platform coordinating ordering, fulfillment, billing, notification, fraud, and analytics
patterns.mechanism: events form explicit contracts while producers and consumers own delivery, idempotency, ordering, replay, and observability
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct request-response or a modular monolith when immediate consistency and operational simplicity dominate
patterns.misuse: event soup, hidden workflows, commands disguised as events, no schema ownership, or assuming the broker guarantees business correctness
patterns.evidence: event lag, duplicate handling, schema compatibility, causal trace completeness, operational components, and recovery
patterns.typescript: versioned event unions, schema packages, transactional outbox, typed consumers, trace context, and idempotent handlers

patterns.name: Model-View-Controller
patterns.problem: interactive presentation concerns need separation among domain state, rendering, and input coordination
patterns.exampleContext: a server-rendered administration console with complex workflows and multiple presentation formats
patterns.mechanism: models own application state, views render representations, and controllers translate input into operations
patterns.simplerAlternative: component-local state or unidirectional reducers for small reactive interfaces
patterns.misuse: fat controllers, passive domain models, views querying databases, framework terminology mistaken for actual boundaries, or duplicated state
patterns.evidence: controller complexity, view testability, model independence, state duplication, and change spread
patterns.typescript: SvelteKit boundary comparison, typed actions, schema-validated input, presentation DTOs, and framework-independent application services

patterns.name: Broker
patterns.problem: distributed components need location-transparent mediation for registration, discovery, invocation, and responses
patterns.exampleContext: a plugin execution grid matching analysis jobs to language-capable remote workers
patterns.mechanism: a broker coordinates service registration, request routing, correlation, protocol, and failure reporting
patterns.simplerAlternative: direct endpoints plus service discovery when centralized mediation adds little value
patterns.misuse: pretending remote calls are local, broker as single failure domain, stale registration, opaque retries, or protocol lock-in
patterns.evidence: routing latency, registry freshness, broker saturation, failure transparency, and recovery
patterns.typescript: typed envelopes, runtime schemas, correlation IDs, AbortSignal deadlines, and explicit remote Result types

patterns.name: Space-Based Architecture
patterns.problem: extreme variable load makes a centralized transactional database the primary bottleneck
patterns.exampleContext: a flash-sale reservation system facing short bursts far above normal traffic
patterns.mechanism: processing units operate over partitioned replicated in-memory state with asynchronous persistence and controlled reconciliation
patterns.simplerAlternative: database scaling, caching, and queues before accepting in-memory distribution and consistency cost
patterns.misuse: marketing ordinary caching as space-based, unclear authority, no recovery model, cross-partition transactions, or memory-cost blindness
patterns.evidence: peak throughput, partition balance, recovery time, persistence lag, lost-state risk, and infrastructure cost
patterns.typescript: typed partition keys, immutable events, worker isolation, versioned state, deterministic recovery, and explicit consistency outcomes

patterns.name: Cell-Based Architecture
patterns.problem: very large multi-tenant systems need bounded blast radius and repeatable horizontal units
patterns.exampleContext: a global SaaS platform assigning tenants to independently scalable regional cells
patterns.mechanism: self-contained cells own compute and data while a thin control plane places tenants and routes traffic
patterns.simplerAlternative: ordinary regional deployment or sharding when blast-radius isolation does not justify duplicated stacks
patterns.misuse: shared dependencies defeating isolation, oversized cells, control plane on the data path, untested evacuation, or uneven tenant placement
patterns.evidence: blast radius, cell saturation, placement balance, evacuation time, shared dependency count, and cost per tenant
patterns.typescript: branded cell and tenant IDs, pure placement functions, versioned routing metadata, typed failover states, and contract-tested cells

patterns.name: Model Router
patterns.problem: incoming model prompts have diverse complexity, latency, and cost requirements that a single static LLM cannot optimally fulfill
patterns.exampleContext: a customer support agent routing simple FAQs to small fast models while delegating complex policy reasoning to frontier reasoning models
patterns.mechanism: a dynamic classifier and policy engine that evaluates prompt complexity, token budgets, SLA targets, and model capabilities to select optimal inference providers
patterns.simplerAlternative: a single capable model or static prompt-to-model mapping when query variance, cost pressure, or traffic volume is low
patterns.misuse: over-engineering routing for uniform workloads, adding unmeasured classification latency, routing sensitive context to unvetted providers, or missing fallback paths
patterns.evidence: average token cost, p95 end-to-end latency, classification accuracy, SLA compliance rate, fallback frequency, and model provider error rates
patterns.typescript: discriminated model capabilities, schema-driven tier selection, typed cost estimators, async fallback chains, and streaming response unions

patterns.name: Tool Circuit Breaker
patterns.problem: unreliable external tool executions or flaky agent function calls waste context tokens, increase latency, and cause agent loop failures
patterns.exampleContext: an autonomous coding or search agent invoking external APIs whose rate limits, network timeouts, or schema drift cause cascading task failure
patterns.mechanism: per-tool failure tracking and state isolation that fast-fails unviable tool invocations, injects synthetic degradation prompts, and guides agent fallback plans
patterns.simplerAlternative: standard distributed circuit breaker when tool invocations do not require agent-visible error context or alternative reasoning paths
patterns.misuse: failing silently without informing the agent reasoning loop, treating valid tool rejections as infrastructural faults, or tripping global agent execution on single tool failure
patterns.evidence: tool invocation success rate, wasted loop iterations, token burn on failed tools, fast-fail recovery time, agent fallback success rate, and mean time to isolate
patterns.typescript: typed tool schemas, discriminated breaker states, synthetic error injections, tool capability registries, and AbortController integration

patterns.name: Semantic Cache
patterns.problem: semantically equivalent natural language queries generate redundant expensive LLM completions and unnecessary latency
patterns.exampleContext: an enterprise Q&A assistant receiving paraphrased user questions that ask for identical policy documentation answers
patterns.mechanism: dense embedding similarity indexing over query vectors with configurable cosine distance thresholds, TTL expiry, and metadata filtering to serve cached responses
patterns.simplerAlternative: exact-match key-value cache (cache-aside) when prompt phrasing is deterministic or strictly structured
patterns.misuse: using loose similarity thresholds causing semantic drift or hallucinated answers, ignoring personalized context, caching volatile time-sensitive queries, or unbounded vector store growth
patterns.evidence: semantic hit rate, token cost savings, p50/p99 query latency reduction, false-match report rate, embedding latency overhead, and cache memory footprint
patterns.typescript: vector similarity math, typed embedding adapters, threshold validation, branded cache keys, metadata filters, and TTL-aware stores
